chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Al-Qasim ibn Urwah, from Bureyd ibn Muawiya, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked him about the owned slave, is his testimony allowed? He said: Yes, the first one who rejected the testimony of the owned slave was so-and-so.
ai.seo_question: Is the testimony of a slave valid in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi affirms the validity of a male slave's (mamluk) testimony, tracing the deviation to a specific historical figure, often identified in Shia tradition as Umar ibn al-Khattab, who introduced the restriction. It highlights the Shia jurisprudential stance that the Prophet’s original practice allowed for such testimony, viewing the later exclusion as a departure from the Sunnah. This ruling underscores the principle that legal capacities are not inherently diminished by social status unless explicitly restricted by divine text.
